name: thing
description: Anything that can be a 3D model. The conventions here apply to every model.
conventions: Units are metres. +Y is up. The front of the model faces +Z (the glTF convention, which three.js's GLTFLoader keeps), so the model's left side is +X.
The origin sits on the ground (y = 0), under the centre of the model or under the point a user will place it by.
Every part that moves gets its own node, with the node origin at its pivot. Use PascalCase names and keep sibling names unique.
Apply scale and rotation before export: scale 1 on every node, no negative scale.
Left and right halves are exact mirror images unless the object is asymmetric by design.
anticipate: A simple collision shape (a box or convex hull), not the visual mesh.
A triangle budget, and LODs for anything that will appear many times.
Few materials: every material is a draw call, so share textures where you can.
pitfalls: A model that is 100 times too big or small (a unit mistake) is the most common error: check the size against the typical range.
A moving part baked into the body mesh cannot be animated later.

name: snowman
description: A snowman: two or three stacked snowballs with a face of coal and a carrot nose, stick arms, and often a hat and a scarf.

parts.name: Base
parts.note: The biggest ball, flattened where it stands in the snow.

parts.name: Head
parts.note: Its node sits at the bottom of the head ball, so the head can turn.

parts.name: Arm
parts.note: A stick pushed into the body; its node sits where it goes in.

scale.source: general knowledge: a garden snowman is about 0.5-2 m tall; the record snowwoman (Bethel, Maine, 2008) was 37 m, far outside this range

conventions: Stands on y = 0 with the face towards +Z.
anticipate: A melting animation: scale the balls down in y over time and lower the head and hat with them.
pitfalls: Balls that only touch at a point look stacked like marbles: let them sink into each other.
A perfectly smooth sphere reads as plastic: snowballs are slightly lumpy and matte.
